title: The storm at sea
hook: crossing to Georgia, John Wesley is terrified; Moravian families sing calmly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herrnhut and the Moravians' watch, one hour each, so the fire never went out. Your line was the watch of prayer.

A ship is crossing the Atlantic, bound for the colony of Georgia. On board is a young Church of England clergyman named John Wesley: serious, disciplined, on his way to be a missionary. He prays on a strict schedule. He fasts. He keeps a careful journal of how he spends his hours. And he is afraid of dying. Also on board are German Moravians, families from the movement we met yesterday, men, women and children. Wesley has been watching them: how humble they are, how willing to do the dirty jobs nobody else wants. Then the weather turns.

Wesley tells it in his journal. The Moravians are holding their evening service, in the middle of the opening psalm, when the sea breaks over the ship, splits the mainsail, and pours in between the decks. A terrible screaming starts among the English passengers. Then, in Wesley's plain sentence: "The Germans calmly sung on." Afterward, Wesley asks one of them if he wasn't afraid. The man answers, "I thank God, no." Weren't the women and children afraid? The man replies, mildly, "No; our women and children are not afraid to die." Wesley writes it all down. He's a clergyman and a missionary who has worked hard at his religion, and he has just watched these families face death with a calm he doesn't have. That gap troubles him, and sends him looking for whatever it is they know. The scene echoes a gospel story. In Mark, Jesus is asleep in a boat during a great storm, and the terrified disciples wake him. He speaks to the wind and the sea, "Peace, be still," and there's a great calm. Then he turns to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" On Wesley's ship, the sea doesn't calm. The storm goes on. What's calm is the singing. The danger is real, and the Moravians are in it with everyone else. They sing in the middle of it, and a frightened young clergyman is paying attention, which is where tomorrow's story begins.

Bring to mind something that frightens you right now, small or large, and let it be there. Then let a steadying song come, a hymn, a psalm, a lullaby someone sang to you, and hum it or hear it in your head while the fear is still in the room. If you pray, let the song be your prayer, or rest with Jesus' words: peace, be still.
John Wesley. The frightened young clergyman who watched Moravian families keep singing while a storm broke over their ship to Georgia.
Your line: they were not afraid. They sang in the storm, not after it. Day eight hundred ninety-three, done.

chat.says: Did the storm stop when the Moravians on Wesley's ship started singing?
options: No, the storm went on; what was calm was the singing, right in the danger.
Yes, the sea grew calm the moment they began their psalm, as in Mark.
They waited to sing until the storm was over, to give thanks.
chat.meaning: On Wesley's ship the sea doesn't calm, as it does in Mark. The danger was real, and the Moravians sang in the middle of it.

'He is afraid of dying': Wesley says this of himself in the journal around this voyage; confirm.
